standard.title: First Nations Rights Campaigns Before 1965
standard.description: the causes of First Nations Australians' campaigns for rights and freedoms before 1965, such as discriminatory legislation and policies, the 1938 Day of Mourning and the Stolen Generations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined First Nations Australians' wartime service and the contradiction between service and denied citizenship (AC9HH10K04). From Y9 they have studied colonisation and its effects on First Nations peoples (AC9HH9K03, K06). They have not yet examined the specific legislative and policy framework that governed First Nations Australians' lives in the 20th century, the early organised campaigns for rights, or the Stolen Generations as a distinct historical phenomenon.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes of First Nations Australians' campaigns for rights and freedoms before 1965, including the discriminatory legislative and policy framework, the significance of the 1938 Day of Mourning, and the impact of the Stolen Generations on the civil rights movement.

nodes.label: The legislative and policy framework of exclusion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the legal and policy framework that governed First Nations Australians' lives in the early-to-mid 20th century, explaining how it structured inequality and motivated campaigns for change.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two specific legislative or policy mechanisms and explain how each restricted First Nations Australians' rights and freedoms.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the legal status of First Nations Australians at Commonwealth and state/territory levels — excluded from the census, restricted from voting, subject to state protection legislation; examine segregation and treatment on missions and reserves; examine the 1937 assimilation policy adopted by the Aboriginal Welfare Conference; explain how these specific mechanisms — not just general racism — created the conditions that made organised campaigns necessary.
wider: Examine how the legislative framework varied across states and territories — analysing whether differences in state laws produced different experiences for First Nations Australians in different jurisdictions

Investigate the role of protection boards and protectors — examining how the administrative apparatus of 'protection' functioned as a system of control over movement, employment, family, and cultural practice
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the specific legislative and policy mechanisms is the prerequisite for understanding why campaigns were necessary and what they were responding to. Students who treat discrimination as general background cannot explain why specific campaigns addressed specific targets, or why the 1967 Referendum (K11) was structurally necessary rather than symbolically sufficient.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations exclusion as general and undifferentiated. Making the specific legislative mechanisms explicit — which rights were denied by which laws, and how each law operated in practice — is the scaffold for understanding why particular campaigns targeted particular changes.

success_criteria: Describes at least two specific legislative or policy mechanisms and explains how each restricted First Nations Australians' rights
Explains the 1937 assimilation policy — what it required and what it meant for First Nations communities
Explains how the specific legislative framework motivated organised campaigns rather than merely caused suffering

nodes.label: Early organised resistance — the AAPA, AAL, and the 1938 Day of Mourning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the significance of early organised campaigns for First Nations rights, including the AAPA, the Australian Aborigines League, and the 1938 Day of Mourning.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the significance of the 1938 Day of Mourning — what it was, why 26 January 1938 was chosen, and what it demanded.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association (AAPA) under Fred Maynard as an early organised political movement; examine William Cooper and the Australian Aborigines League; explain the 1938 Day of Mourning — its organisation by Jack Patten and William Cooper, the choice of 26 January 1938 (150th anniversary of British arrival) as the occasion, the demands made, and its significance as the first national Indigenous rights meeting; explain how these movements established the model of organised political campaigning that later movements built on.
wider: Examine the international influences on early First Nations political organising — including the influence of Marcus Garvey's pan-African movement on Fred Maynard and the AAPA — analysing how global movements for racial equality shaped Australian First Nations activism

Investigate William Cooper's 1938 petition to the German consulate protesting Kristallnacht — examining what this reveals about how First Nations activists connected their own struggle to international human rights concerns
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The international influences on early First Nations activism — particularly the Garvey connection and Cooper's Holocaust protest — are analytically rich and largely unknown to students. They reveal the sophisticated political consciousness of early activists and connect domestic history to global movements.

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple early organisations — AAPA, AAL, Day of Mourning — prevents the reduction of pre-1965 activism to a single event. Building a repertoire of early campaigns shows that organised resistance had a long history before the 1960s Freedom Rides, which is the key correction to the common misconception that rights activism began in the 1960s.

success_criteria: Explains the significance of the 1938 Day of Mourning — including the choice of date and the demands made
Identifies at least two early organisations involved in First Nations rights campaigns and explains each organisation's approach
Explains how early campaigns established the model for later organised activism

nodes.label: The Stolen Generations — policy, experience, and lasting impact
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the policy basis for the removal of First Nations children, describe the experiences of those removed, and explain how the Stolen Generations influenced the civil rights movement.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the policy basis for child removal; describe the experiences of removed children using at least one primary source; explain at least one way the Stolen Generations influenced the civil rights movement.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the assimilation policy as the ideological basis for child removal — the premise that First Nations children should be absorbed into white society; examine the experiences of children removed from families — separation from family and country, denial of language and culture, exposure to abuse in institutions; use primary sources including accounts from Stolen Generations members; explain how the Stolen Generations created a generation of activists who personally experienced the consequences of discriminatory policy and channelled that experience into organised resistance from the 1960s.
wider: Examine the Stolen Generations across different states and territories — analysing how the policy operated differently in different jurisdictions and how this affected the experiences of those removed

Investigate how the Stolen Generations have been commemorated and addressed — examining the Bringing Them Home report (1997), the first Sorry Day, and the Apology (2008) as a sequence of recognition, connecting to K11
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The connection between personal experience of the Stolen Generations and later civil rights activism is a rich causal argument that connects K09 forward to K10 and K11. Primary source work with Stolen Generations testimony also develops substantial AC9HH10S03 and S04 skills.

response_modes.reason: Students need to understand the Stolen Generations as a policy — with an internal ideological logic — not merely as an atrocity. Making the assimilation premise explicit — and then connecting it to the lived experiences of those removed — builds the causal argument for why the Stolen Generations became a driver of civil rights activism.

success_criteria: Explains the assimilation policy as the ideological basis for child removal — not merely that removal occurred
Describes the experiences of removed children using at least one primary source
Explains at least one mechanism through which the Stolen Generations influenced the later civil rights movement
